slides.title: Why subword tokens beat words and characters
slides.body:
Before a language model sees text, the text gets cut into **tokens**. There are three obvious ways to do it:

- **Word-level**: one token per word. Vocabulary explodes (English alone has hundreds of thousands of forms), and any word the model didn't see in training becomes `<UNK>`. Misspellings, names, novel compounds — all unknown.
- **Character-level**: one token per character. Vocabulary is tiny (~100 for ASCII), but sequences become 4-5× longer for the same text. Models burn most of their compute predicting whitespace.
- **Subword (BPE)**: a fixed-size vocabulary of frequent character sequences. Common words get a single token; rare words decompose into pieces the model has seen elsewhere.

BPE is the compromise that won. GPT-2/3/4, LLaMA, and most other modern LLMs use it (or a close variant like SentencePiece).

slides.title: The merge-pair algorithm
slides.body:
BPE training is greedy and simple:

1. **Start** with a vocabulary of all individual characters.
2. **Count** every adjacent pair of tokens in the corpus.
3. **Merge** the most frequent pair into a new token; add it to the vocabulary.
4. **Repeat** for N merges (typical N: 30k–100k).

With English text, the first merges produce things like `t h → th`, `i n → in`, `e r → er`. After thousands of merges, common whole words emerge as single tokens.

At inference, the same merges are applied greedily: longest-match first.

```
Merge 1: 'th' (most frequent pair: 't'+'h')
Merge 2: 'in' (most frequent pair: 'i'+'n')
Merge 3: 'the' (most frequent pair: 'th'+'e')
...
```

question.question: A BPE tokenizer trained on English encounters the word `tokenization` for the first time. What's the most likely outcome?
options: The word is replaced with a single `<UNK>` token
The word is split into characters: `t o k e n i z a t i o n`
The word is split into subword pieces like `token` + `ization`
The word is added to the vocabulary on the fly
question.explanation: BPE never sees `<UNK>` because every character is in the base vocabulary, and any sequence of characters can be encoded by some sequence of merges. Common subwords like `token` and `ization` are likely already in the vocabulary, so the word decomposes cleanly.

slides.title: Tokenizer surprises
slides.body:
Two facts that bite people in production:

**Leading spaces are part of the token.** `" the"` and `"the"` are different tokens in most BPE tokenizers. This is why prompts that start mid-sentence sometimes produce off-by-one weirdness — the model hasn't seen `"the"` (no leading space) often, so it treats it as rare.

**Numbers are split inconsistently.** `"3.14159"` might tokenize as `["3", ".", "14", "159"]` or `["3", ".1", "4159"]` depending on the tokenizer. This is one of the reasons LLMs are bad at arithmetic — the digits don't have stable identities.

If your model is failing at character-level tasks (counting letters, reversing strings, syllable rhyming), suspect tokenization first.

question.question: A model uses a 50,000-token BPE vocabulary trained on English. Roughly how many tokens does a typical 1,000-word English document take?
question.explanation: The rule of thumb for English BPE is ~0.75 words per token, or about 4 characters per token. This is why a 'Tokenizer' tab will show 1,300 tokens for what feels like 1,000 words — leading spaces, punctuation, and rare-word splits add up.

slides.title: Where to next
slides.body:
BPE is the workhorse, but it's not the only option. **WordPiece** (BERT) uses likelihood-based merging instead of frequency. **Unigram** (T5, sentencepiece default) starts from a large vocabulary and prunes. **Tiktoken** (GPT-4) is BPE with byte-level fallback, so any sequence of bytes can be tokenized — even non-UTF-8 input.

Once you have tokens, the next step is [[embeddings]]: each token id becomes a `d_model`-dimensional vector that the rest of the network operates on. Then [[attention]] takes over.

In practice, you'll rarely train a tokenizer from scratch. You'll inherit one from a base model — and then debug the surprising things it does to your inputs.

question.question: Explain in 2-3 sentences why BPE outperforms both word-level and character-level tokenization for modern LLMs. Touch on vocabulary size, out-of-vocabulary handling, and sequence length.

rubricCriteria.description: Mentions BPE keeps vocabulary fixed-size (vs unbounded for word-level)
Mentions BPE handles unseen words by decomposing into subwords (vs word-level UNK)
Mentions BPE sequences are shorter than character-level for the same text
